blurb: Ways to detect and defeat drones — jamming, spoofing, lasers, high-power microwave, guns, interceptors, and nets — plus the wider electronic warfare toolkit, compared on effectiveness, collateral risk, and cost exchange.
question: How do you stop a drone without spending more than it cost?
title: Counter-UAS and Electronic Warfare: A Practical Reference
lede: Shooting down a $500 drone with a $1M missile is a win that you cannot afford twice. This guide covers {{N_ENTRIES}} counter-drone and electronic warfare approaches, compared on what they actually stop, what they break when they miss, and how the cost exchange works out.

facets.label: Works on
facets.tip: What the approach actually defeats. Group 1–2 covers small drones under 25 kg; Group 3–5 covers tactical and larger UAS; Swarms means many simultaneous targets; Cruise missiles covers subsonic one-way attack weapons; Aircraft covers crewed aircraft and the radar-guided weapons aimed at them.

facets.label: Effectiveness
facets.tip: How reliably it works against the threats it is designed for, in field conditions rather than on a test range. Limited = works sometimes, against some models · Situational = depends heavily on conditions and threat type · Reliable = works when properly employed · High = very high probability of defeat per engagement.

facets.label: Collateral
facets.tip: Risk to everything that is not the target: falling debris, rounds that keep travelling, interference with friendly GNSS and radios, and effects on civil aviation and infrastructure. This is usually what decides whether a system can be used in a populated area at all.

facets.label: Exchange
facets.tip: Cost per engagement against the cost of the target it defeats. Unfavorable = you spend more than the attacker · Even = roughly comparable · Favorable = you spend less · Strongly favorable = you spend a small fraction, usually because the shot is electricity or ammunition rather than a missile.

facets.label: System cost
facets.tip: Directional acquisition cost for one deployed system, excluding the magazine of ammunition or interceptors. A handheld jammer and a shipboard laser differ by four orders of magnitude, which is why the cost-per-shot argument has to be read alongside this.
